extracted.intended_audience: newspaper editors, reporters, journalism researchers, and writing coaches
extracted.subtask_description: Field-experiment guidance and evaluative criteria for comparing four newswriting modes (Traditional, Narrative, Radical Clarity, Point of View) on reader outcomes (reading, involvement, quality, knowledge) and for choosing/combining styles for newspaper stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional (inverted-pyramid) mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the inverted pyramid: a compelling lead with subsequent material arranged in descending order of importance; neutral tone; more telling than showing; designed for production (can be shortened by deleting from the bottom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: suits production needs, familiar to readers and editors; tends to score high on perceived 'Quality' among accustomed, well-educated readers. Cons: may assume more background knowledge than readers have, becomes less interesting deeper in the story, places context late (nut-graph often buried), and may perform poorly on getting readers to read beyond the opening or to learn, especially among younger/less-educated/infrequent readers. Used in the study as the control form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Tells a story with characters acting in time sequences (beginning, middle, end); reveals motives through actions and quotations; emphasizes showing over telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: familiar storytelling expectations, broad population accessibility; in the experiment it was most effective at keeping readers reading and had the best overall net performance (+8). It can directly lead to learning for some readers (direct path from reading to knowledge). Cons: in this study it often failed to increase 'Involvement' with issues (did not necessarily make readers care about issue/action). Editors are encouraged to use storytelling components to capture interest even if not adopting full narrative mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical Clarity mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranges material to maximize reader understanding and explains whatever the reader might need explained; background and context appear early; may use second person; defines terms and explains motives explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: orients reader immediately, reduces need to 'read between the lines'; in the study it helped some groups (least-educated read more and rated quality high) and produced learning via reading or involvement rather than quality judgments. Cons: can become a boring outline if overused; did not produce standout positive effects overall and did not support hypothesis that it would maximize knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of View mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Tells the story with a clear viewpoint; tone approaches editorializing; uses non-inverted shapes with a forceful ending to leave the writer's central point; may use second person; attempts persuasion by showing rather than telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: can increase 'Involvement' for some readers and (in the study) resulted in involvement and learning for some subgroups (men, least-educated). Cons: performed worst on perceived 'Quality' (eight of eleven subgroups rated it substantially lower); readers often rated its quality low and read less of it. Use cautiously; may work for persuasion-goals but risks lowered perceived journalistic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading (dependent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of how much of the treatment story the reader read: whether they read the first few paragraphs, more than the first few paragraphs, or most or all of it (interviews were terminated for those who had read only headline or lead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an outcome to judge engagement/scan-to-deep-read; in path analysis Reading is an antecedent to Knowledge and interacts differently with other variables depending on mode (e.g., Narrative can lead directly from Reading to Knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement (dependent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor composed of four items (each rated 1 to 10): 'How much did you care about what happened in the article?' 'How much did you connect the article to other issues or your own experiences?' 'How much did reading this article make you want to find out more about issues like this?' and 'How much did reading this article make you want to get more directly involved in issues like this?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures motivational/behavioral engagement beyond mere reading. Not correlated with Quality in this study (readers could be involved without rating quality high). Different modes affected Involvement differently (Point of View and Narrative expected to score higher on this, though results varied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (dependent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor composed of two items (each rated 1 to 10): 'How would you rate how well the (treatment) article was written?' and 'On the same scale, how balanced and accurate was the writing for this article?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects readers' perceptions of journalistic standards; Traditional mode tended to score highest on Quality among accustomed/readers, while Point of View scored lowest on Quality. Quality can mediate the effect of Reading on Knowledge for some modes (e.g., Traditional required high perceived Quality before learning occurred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge (dependent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite score from four true-or-false questions related to basic factual information contained in all four versions of a story; higher number correct = higher standardized Knowledge score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to capture actual learning from the story. Hypothesis anticipated Radical Clarity would maximize Knowledge, but results showed different modes produce different paths to Knowledge (Narrative had two paths, including a direct Reading→Knowledge path).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls for comparability of story variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraints applied across all four versions each day: identical photographs/graphics, identical headlines and identical subheads, same story length, same 'jump' location inside the section, prominent placement (over the fold) in local section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These production-level controls are required to isolate writing-mode effects from layout, headline, photo, length, and placement influences. For production/testing, ensure all non-writing elements are held constant when comparing styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation and counterbalancing of reporters and zones
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters rotated through all four writing modes and circulation zones over the four days; each zone received every mode over the study so each zone and reporter experienced all treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to control for reporter skill/talent and zone-specific readership biases. When evaluating writing modes in a field setting, rotate authors and publication zones to avoid confounding talent or local preferences with mode effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection and survey screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily telephone surveys sampled by cluster (carrier routes) from the newspaper's subscriber lists with equal representation from each zone; respondents were screened and only those who had read the treatment story completed the schedule. A supplemental technical-college sample (210 adult students) was included to better represent younger, less-educated, less-loyal readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For naturalistic readership evaluation, sample readers without prior recruitment/cueing, screen for actual exposure, and consider supplemental targeted samples to include theoretically important subgroups underrepresented among subscribers. Control for differences due to survey setting (cross-sectional telephone vs. classroom questionnaire) in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scoring conventions (standardization and 'substantial' difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: All four dependent-variable scores were standardized to range between -1 and +1 with the group mean at zero. A difference was deemed 'substantial' if it deviated from the group mean by more than 5 percent of the possible variation for that dependent variable; asterisks mark substantial values in tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standardized scoring to compare across measures; pre-specify thresholds for practical (substantial) effects (here >5% of scale range) rather than rely only on strict p<.05 significance in exploratory field work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specified hypotheses about mode effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Five main-effect hypotheses: H1) Knowledge highest for Radical Clarity; H2) Involvement highest for Narrative and Point of View; H3) Quality highest for Traditional and lowest for Point of View; H4) Reading highest for Narrative, Traditional lowest; H5) Traditional will not score better than alternatives. Plus interaction hypothesis HG: younger, less-educated, less-frequent readers will score higher with Narrative and Radical Clarity and lower with Traditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clear, testable expectations about how modes will affect each dependent variable and about interactions with reader demographics; use these as evaluation criteria but be prepared for mixed/contradictory real-world results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path-analysis criterion: routes from Reading to Knowledge differ by mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Regression/path analyses showed different mediational structures: Traditional required high perceived Quality before Knowledge; Narrative had two paths (Quality→Knowledge and Reading→Knowledge direct); Radical Clarity led to Knowledge via Reading or Involvement with little role for Quality; Point of View produced Knowledge only via Quality or Involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a writing mode, consider desired route to learning: if goal is pure information transfer, Radical Clarity or Narrative may be preferable; if goal is to induce caring/action, select modes that produce Involvement. Use path-analysis thinking to align writing structure with intended outcome (reading, learning, involvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection for testing or adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose ordinary local-news 'one-day' stories typical of local sections (not splashy front-section leads or late-breaking items); select topics likely to interest readers equally across zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate writing modes fairly, use stories that are representative of routine local reporting. Avoid late-breaking items that require different logistics or extreme writing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial production recommendations (combining modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice for editors: encourage storytelling components; combine modes creatively (e.g., use a narrative to capture interest and a 'radically clear' sidebar to communicate hard information; include a summary box/nut graph in narrative pieces so scanners can find essence early).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single style is superior for all goals and audiences; match style to the story's primary objective (induce readership, convey information, entertain, move to action) and consider hybrid formats (sidebars, summary boxes) to meet multiple outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience segmentation and tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent variables to consider when evaluating/writing: age (trichotomized at 30 and 64), education (less than HS; HS diploma; more than HS), and readership frequency (0-3 days/wk, 4-6 days/wk, 7 days/wk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different demographic/readership subgroups respond differently to modes (e.g., Narrative pulled younger readers in; Radical Clarity helped least-educated read more). Tailor mode selection or combinations to target audience segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement item-level practice (factor construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Involvement and Quality variables were constructed via factor analysis from multiple questionnaire items (Involvement: four 1–10 items; Quality: two 1–10 items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When operationalizing subjective outcomes like involvement and quality, use multiple items and factor analysis to create reliable composite measures rather than single-item judgments.
